chapter_theme: Raising one's people is the highest greatness. It requires ceaseless effort and knowledge, draws divine help and willing kin, ignores season and pride, and costs the one who does it his own bodily ease. A family with no one to carry it falls.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its causes (1021-1022), divine support (1023-1024), the honour it gains (1025-1027), how it is done (1028-1029), and the fate of a family without such a person (1030). Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take குடி as one's own lineage; Kalaignar repeatedly reads it as the people who depend on one, குடிமக்கள், which turns a family ethic into a public one.

1021.reading: No greatness has more dignity than that of one who says 'I will not stay my hand from the work'.
1021.nuance: The verse says only கருமம், and family comes from the chapter's title. Parimelazhagar rejects two rival readings, one's own work and others' work, the second because serving others isn't leadership. Greatness here sits in the declaration (என்னும்), before any result.

1022.reading: By long-continued work in the two things called effort and mature knowledge, the family is extended.
1022.nuance: நீள்வினையால் நீளும் is a chime, in which the long labour lengthens the line.

positions.position: குடி is one's own family, and it rises.
குடி is the people attached to him, whose pride rises.

1023.reading: For one who says 'I will raise my people', தெய்வம் tucks up its garment and goes ahead on its own.
1023.nuance: The image of tightened dress is homely and physical: the divine as a worker who gets ready to help.

positions.position: The deity is said to lead, and leading is an act ascribed to destiny (நியதி).
What is called divine action is the power of nature.

1024.reading: For those who work without delay for their people, the end arrives by itself, without deliberation.
1024.nuance: The agent is unnamed. Parimelazhagar supplies the deity of 1023, while Manakkudavar supplies the man's good deeds (நல்வினை), and Kalaignar leaves success to come by itself. Each fills the gap to suit his view.

1025.reading: The world gathers around one who lives faultlessly raising his people, as kin.
1025.nuance: The chime of சுற்றம் and சுற்றும் turns the noun into what kin do. Parimelazhagar's motive for this is unsentimental: people come for their own benefit.

1026.reading: What's called good manliness is making oneself capable of ruling the house one was born to.
1026.nuance: நல்லாண்மை and இல்லாண்மை chime. Parimelazhagar says the adjective நல் is there to exclude the warrior's manliness. Kalaignar reverses the sense: one who rules well brings pride to his birth-family, so it isn't about ruling the family.

1027.reading: As with the stout-hearted in battle, the burden among kin falls on the capable.
1027.nuance: The commentators stress that many enter the field and many are born in a family: it isn't that others are forbidden, but that it falls to whoever can carry it. A question of ability, not of seniority.

1028.reading: Those who raise their people have no season; if they idle and think about மானம், it will be ruined.

positions.position: மானம் is the pride of asking 'why must I alone suffer while the rest are comfortable?'
It is being shaken by degrading attacks made on oneself.

1029.reading: Is the body of one who covers his household against fault only a vessel for suffering?
1029.nuance: Parimelazhagar treats this as a pointed remark and not self-pity: the man accepts it, since the family's rise is his reward.

positions.position: மறைத்தல் is shielding, as with a shield against spears: he protects them from the three kinds of suffering.
positions.quote: மூவகைத் துன்பமும் உறற்பாலதாய தன் குடியை அவை உறாமற்காக்க முயல்வானது உடம்பு

positions.position: மறைத்தல் is concealing the failings found among kin.
positions.quote: சுற்றத்தார் மாட்டு உளதாகிய குறையை மறைக்கக் கருதுவான் உடம்பு

1030.reading: When trouble cuts it at the foot, a family with no good person to prop it will fall.
1030.nuance: A tree image is implied: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar supply the axe. They take நல்லாள் as a good man (ஆண்மகன்), while Kalaignar has anyone with the ability. The same word names a personified good woman in 924 and 1040; here it divides as நல் ஆள், 'good person', which doesn't itself specify a man.

links.note: The same words appear with opposite force. In 380 fate comes first (தான்முந் துறும்), defeating whatever one devises (சூழினும்). In 1023 the divine comes first (தான்முந் துறும்) for the one who resolves, and 1024 adds that the end comes without deliberating (சூழாமல்). Priority over human planning works against effort in one and for it in the other.
619 says that effort pays even when the divine doesn't help. 1023 takes up the other case: effort draws the divine to help. Together they cover both options and in each effort wins.

467 says deliberate and then resolve, and that deliberating afterwards is a fault. 1024 says that for those who work without delay for their people, the outcome comes without deliberating. The two can be reconciled only by treating family work as a special case.
Both use the same play on சுற்றம் and சுற்றுதல். In 525 giving and sweet speech surround one with layers of kin, and 1025 extends this until the whole world gathers around as kin.
148's பேராண்மை is not looking at another's wife, and 1026's நல்லாண்மை is ruling one's house. The Kural keeps coining compound forms of manliness that exclude combat, as Parimelazhagar notes here.

481 says that a king needs the right time, like a crow beating an owl by day. Parimelazhagar explicitly cites 481 at 1028 to mark the exception: one who raises his family needs no season. Timing is wisdom for conquest but an excuse for duty.
Under Manakkudavar's reading of 1029 the two use the same verb, மறைத்தல்: greatness hides others' weakness, and so does the family's support. He bears the cost in his body.
Both see the body as a place for suffering to land: a target in 627 and a vessel in 1029. For 627 this insight is what frees one from distress, and for 1029 the suffering is chosen on others' behalf.

source_issues: 1022: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1023: Manakkudavar's text has what appear to be transcription errors: யோபுவன் and படிதற்றல்.
1021: Pope's gloss adds 'to raise my family', from the chapter's theme.
1028: Manakkudavar's gloss takes மானம் as a fault arising from raising the family, and its wording seems unclear, so it wasn't used as a position.
